denomFacts/fact-33000-protestant/claim: There are 33,000 Protestant denominations, proving that sola scriptura leads to endless division.
denomFacts/fact-33000-protestant/answer: No. The 33,000 figure covered all Christian bodies, including 242 Catholic and 781 Orthodox entries, counted country by country. Protestants (as the Encyclopedia defined them) accounted for only about 9,000, and most of the total came from independent churches.
denomFacts/fact-33000-protestant/explana:
The claim became popular in Catholic apologetics in the 1990s and 2000s as an argument that, without a teaching authority, Protestant reliance on the Bible alone produces endless fragmentation. It has also been used by sceptics to argue that Christianity as a whole is incoherent.

The source, the World Christian Encyclopedia (2001), does not support it. Its total of roughly 33,800 included every megabloc: Independents (about 22,000), Protestants (about 9,000), 'marginal' Christians (about 1,600), Orthodox (781), Catholics (242) and Anglicans (168). Even those numbers count national organisations, not distinct doctrinal positions.

Catholic writers themselves have urged people to stop using the figure. Scott Eric Alt's article in the National Catholic Register, 'We Need to Stop Saying That There Are 33,000 Protestant Denominations', pointed out that the number rests on a very loose definition of denomination and that by the same method Catholicism is 242 denominations. Catholic Answers and other Catholic writers have made the same point.

The underlying debate is real: Protestantism has indeed produced more separate organisations than the Catholic or Orthodox churches, and the question of how Scripture is authoritatively interpreted remains a genuine point of disagreement. But the argument is better made without a misquoted statistic.

denomFacts/fact-how-many-christians/ques: How many Christians are there and how are they divided?
denomFacts/fact-how-many-christians/clai: About a third of humanity is Christian, and about half of all Christians are Catholic.
denomFacts/fact-how-many-christians/answ: Broadly yes. The Center for the Study of Global Christianity estimates about 2.6 billion Christians in 2025 (32.3 per cent of the world), of whom about 1.27 billion are Catholic, 629 million Protestant, 409 million Independent and about 290 million Orthodox. Pew Research gives a lower total of 2.3 billion (28.8 per cent) for 2020.
denomFacts/fact-how-many-christians/expl:
Different counters use different methods. The Center for the Study of Global Christianity (Gordon-Conwell), which publishes the World Christian Database, combines church membership figures, censuses and surveys, and includes children and people who identify as Christian without belonging to a church. Pew Research Center relies chiefly on censuses and large surveys of self-identification, and counted about 2.18 billion Christians in 2010 and 2.3 billion in 2020.

The Catholic Church's own statistics count baptised members and give a higher figure, 1.42 billion at the end of 2024 (17.8 per cent of the world). Many of these baptised Catholics no longer practise or have joined other churches, which is why independent estimates are lower.

The CSGC divides Christians into megablocs: Catholics; Protestants (now including Anglicans); Independents (churches that do not belong to the historic families, such as many African, Chinese and Pentecostal churches); Orthodox (Eastern and Oriental together); plus smaller categories. Some people are counted in more than one (the 'doubly affiliated'), so the parts do not exactly sum to the total.

Across the different methods the pattern is stable: Catholics are roughly half of all Christians, Protestants and Independents together a little over 40 per cent, and Orthodox about 11–12 per cent.

denomFacts/fact-largest-churches/questio: Which are the largest single churches?
denomFacts/fact-largest-churches/claim: After the Catholic Church, the largest churches are the Orthodox, the Anglican Communion and the Assemblies of God.
denomFacts/fact-largest-churches/answer: The Catholic Church, with about 1.42 billion baptised members (2024), is by far the largest single church. After it, the comparison depends on whether one counts communions and federations—the Eastern Orthodox, the Anglican Communion (about 85 million commonly cited), the World Assemblies of God Fellowship (about 89 million in 2025) and the Lutheran World Federation (about 78 million in 2023)—or single national churches such as the Russian or Ethiopian Orthodox churches.
denomFacts/fact-largest-churches/explana:
Only the Catholic Church is a single, centrally governed church on a global scale. The Eastern Orthodox are a communion of self-governing churches, the largest being the Russian Orthodox Church; Pew (2017) estimated about 260 million Orthodox Christians worldwide, including the Oriental Orthodox, around 100 million of them in Russia.

The Anglican Communion is a fellowship of 42 autonomous provinces; its often-cited figure of about 85 million rests largely on baptismal rolls in England and Nigeria. The World Assemblies of God Fellowship, a cooperative fellowship of national councils rather than one church, reported about 88.9 million adherents in 2025. The Lutheran World Federation's member churches reported 78.4 million members in 2023, and the World Communion of Reformed Churches speaks of about 100 million in its member churches, but both are federations of independent churches.

Among single national churches, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church (about 32 million adherents in Ethiopia's 2007 census), the Church of Nigeria (Anglican) and Brazil's Assembleias de Deus are among the largest. Baptists, united loosely in the Baptist World Alliance, count about 47 million baptised members (2021) in 241 separate unions and conventions.

Figures are not strictly comparable: some churches count baptised infants, others only adult members or active publishers, and self-reported totals are rarely audited.

denomFacts/fact-fastest-growing/claim: Pentecostal, charismatic and independent churches in the Global South are the fastest-growing part of Christianity.
denomFacts/fact-fastest-growing/answer: Yes, with caveats about definitions. Pentecostals and charismatics grew from under a million in 1900 to about 664 million in 2025, and Independents from about 9 million to about 409 million (CSGC). Growth is concentrated in Africa and Asia, while Catholics grew by about 0.6 per cent a year in 2020–25.
denomFacts/fact-fastest-growing/explanat:
The Center for the Study of Global Christianity's long-term series shows the most dramatic change of the last century: the rise of 'renewalists'—Pentecostals, charismatics in older churches, and independent neo-charismatics. Their share of all Christians has risen from almost nothing in 1900 to about a quarter today.

The Independent megabloc, which includes African Initiated Churches, Chinese house churches and independent Pentecostal networks, has grown more than forty-fold since 1900. Evangelicals, defined as members of evangelical churches, numbered about 420 million in 2025. By contrast, the Catholic and Orthodox populations are growing more slowly than the world population as a whole.

Regional growth matters as much as denominational. Africa had about 754 million Christians in 2025 and is growing fastest, through both high birth rates and conversion; Asia has about 417 million, and growth in China, India and Iran is significant though hard to measure. In Europe and North America many historic churches are shrinking.

The figures have limitations: 'Pentecostal/charismatic' overlaps with every other megabloc, and surveys in some countries (notably China) cannot be verified. Pew's projections also stress demography: much of Christianity's future growth is driven by birth rates in sub-Saharan Africa rather than conversions.
denomFacts/fact-where-christians-live/qu: Where do most Christians live now?
denomFacts/fact-where-christians-live/cl: Most Christians now live in the Global South—Africa, Latin America and Asia.
denomFacts/fact-where-christians-live/an: Yes. According to the Center for the Study of Global Christianity, 69 per cent of Christians lived in the Global South in 2025, compared with less than a fifth in 1900, and the share is projected to reach 78 per cent by 2050. Africa now has more Christians than any other continent.
denomFacts/fact-where-christians-live/ex:
In 1900 about four in five Christians lived in Europe and North America. During the twentieth century, missionary expansion, conversion and population growth in Africa, Latin America and Asia shifted the centre of gravity of world Christianity southwards, a change described by Andrew Walls, Lamin Sanneh and Philip Jenkins.

The CSGC estimated about 754 million Christians in Africa and about 620 million in Latin America in 2025, with about 417 million in Asia. The Catholic Church's own statistics for 2024 show that 20.3 per cent of Catholics now live in Africa, slightly more than in Europe (20.2 per cent), while the Americas hold 47.7 per cent.

The largest Christian populations by country include the United States, Brazil, Mexico, the Philippines, Russia, Nigeria, China and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Pew Research Center's 2025 report found that in 2020 sub-Saharan Africa had overtaken Europe as the region with the most Christians.

The shift changes what 'typical' Christianity looks like: younger, poorer, more often Pentecostal or charismatic, more conservative on moral questions, and often living as a minority alongside Muslims, Hindus or Buddhists.
